borders.before: the lecturer's welcome, personal background, and lecture learning objectives
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as a genetic, evolutionary disease requiring a permissive microenvironment
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is strictly procedural and introductory lecture framing, whereas Subtopic 2 begins the substantive scientific content of the lecture.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no reason to move the border because Subtopic 1 contains only preliminary framing and Subtopic 2 immediately begins the core definitions.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would conflate administrative course framing with the primary scientific definitions of cancer etiology.

borders.before: broad population-level epidemiological patterns and the philosophical debate around bad luck versus environmental causes
borders.after: specific biological and infectious agents (e.g. H. pylori, EBV, HPV) and their molecular carcinogenic mechanisms
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopics 2 through 6 address high-level concepts and population epidemiology, while Subtopic 7 transitions into detailed molecular and biological mechanisms of specific carcinogens.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 6 belongs with the general epidemiological overview, and Subtopic 7 clearly initiates the survey of specific causal agents, making 7 the natural break.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining them would blur the distinction between broad epidemiological framing and specific molecular mechanisms of individual agents.

borders.before: a summary of direct and indirect mechanisms of DNA damage, promoters, and tissue specificity
borders.after: methods for proving carcinogenicity, starting with mutational signature analysis from whole-genome sequencing
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 provides a complete summary of the biological mechanisms discussed in the preceding section, while Subtopic 18 turns to the methodological question of how carcinogenicity is experimentally proven.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 explicitly summarizes the previous mechanistic concepts and introduces no methods of its own, so the border must fall right after it at Subtopic 18.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would mix the biological mechanisms of tumorigenesis with experimental and epidemiological detection methodologies.

borders.before: in vitro Ames mutagenicity testing and its limitations in accounting for whole-body microenvironments
borders.after: concluding summary points and practical risk-benefit analysis for everyday lifestyle choices
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 21 completes the discussion of experimental assays, while Subtopic 22 serves as the lecture's closing takeaway and wrap-up.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 is squarely about toxicological assays, and Subtopic 22 is purely closing remarks and applause, so no move is warranted.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would improperly merge the concluding lecture wrap-up with a specific laboratory assay.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2 to 4 explore biological predispositions and environmental hazards, whereas Subtopic 5 turns to public understanding and the Tomasetti/Vogelstein 'bad luck' debate.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 to 6 together form a single conceptual introduction addressing the overarching question of what drives cancer, contrasting intrinsic bad luck and genetics with environmental and epidemiological risks.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 7 to 13 focus primarily on direct and indirect mutagens (infectious agents, diet, UV, hydrocarbons), whereas Subtopic 14 introduces non-mutagenic promoters and the Berenbaum two-stage model.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 7 through 17 constitute a continuous catalog of chemical, physical, and biological agents and their roles as initiators or promoters, which are unified and summarized together in Subtopic 17.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 18 and 19 deal with genomic signatures and human biobank epidemiology, while Subtopics 20 and 21 focus on experimental animal and in vitro toxicological testing.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 through 21 form a coherent suite of methodologies (genomics, epidemiology, in vivo toxicology, and in vitro Ames testing) used to determine and prove carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Lecture introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic introduces the lecturer, sets the course context, and outlines the core learning objectives.

topics.label: Cancer etiology: bad luck, genetics, and environmental exposure
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore the foundational drivers of cancer by examining the interplay between intrinsic random mutations, inherited genetic predispositions, and environmental risks supported by epidemiological data.

topics.label: Mechanisms of chemical, physical, and biological carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain the molecular and cellular mechanisms through which infectious agents, direct and metabolized chemical mutagens, radiation, and non-mutagenic promoters initiate and drive tumor formation.

topics.label: Methodologies for identifying and proving carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail the genomic, epidemiological, animal, and in vitro experimental tools used to establish causal links between exposures and cancer.

topics.label: Conclusion and risk-benefit analysis
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic concludes the lecture with key summary points on environmental risk and the practical risk-benefit decisions involved in daily life.
